The Story of Worthy Giving

I bow to Lord Jina, the world-teacher, and I write the story related to worthy giving (patra-dan).

May the pure word of Jina, born from the moon-like face of the Lord, help me cross the great ocean of knowledge. I bow with devotion to those monk-jewels who hold right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, who are passionless, free from attachment to possessions, and who are the cause of attaining worldly and liberation happiness.

The ancient teachers have divided charity into four parts: food-giving, medicine-giving, knowledge-giving, and fearlessness-giving. These alone are pure charities. If these are given to worthy recipients, their fruit multiplies infinitely, like a banyan seed sown in good soil. Just as water from a single well goes into many trees and transforms into various forms, so too the fruit of charity differs according to the worthiness of the recipient. Therefore, one should give to the best recipients possible.

Among all recipients, those who have taken refuge in Jain dharma should be considered worthy, not others. For when one has obtained a wish-fulfilling tree, what use are others? In Jain dharma, three types of recipients are described: the supreme recipient — the monk; the medium recipient — the vowed shravaka; and the lowest recipient — the non-vowed right-faith householder. The happiness attained by worthy souls through giving to these three types of recipients cannot be described by me. But briefly understand that all excellent happiness — wealth, wife, children, food, enjoyment, and the positions of Indra, Nagendra, Vidyadhara, Chakravartin, the company of good souls, and increasing prosperity day by day — all these are attained through the fruit of worthy giving. Not only this, but through the fruit of worthy giving, liberation too becomes attainable. King Shreyans attained liberation through the fruit of giving alone.

Knowing the inconceivable fruit of worthy giving, the wise should certainly draw their attention toward it. The names of all those good souls who have attained fruit through worthy giving cannot be enumerated by anyone except Lord Jina. How then can I, a foolish human, speak or write about them? The Acharyas have given such examples...

This story teaches that the worthiness of the recipient determines the fruit of charity. Giving to those who practise Jain dharma — monks, vowed laymen, and right-faith householders — yields the greatest spiritual benefit. The wise should carefully choose worthy recipients for their charity, for this transforms a simple act of giving into a powerful spiritual practice that leads to both worldly happiness and ultimate liberation.
